title: Variance (covariance and contravariance versus TypeScript)
hook: IEnumerable<string> can be treated as IEnumerable<object> because T only comes out. IList<string> cannot become IList<object> because you could add a Dog to what was a list of cats. TypeScript's structural rules are looser — do not import them into C#.

blocks.text: Variance describes whether a generic type can substitute a more derived or more base type argument. Covariance (out T) applies when T only flows out — producers. IEnumerable<out T> lets IEnumerable<string> be used as IEnumerable<object>. Contravariance (in T) applies when T only flows in — consumers. Action<in T> lets Action<object> be used as Action<string>. Class and struct type parameters are invariant — List<string> is never a List<object>. Only interfaces and delegates declare variance, and only for reference types.

entries.plainDefinition: A producer: T only appears in output positions, so a narrower T can substitute for a wider one.
entries.example: IEnumerable<string> assigned to IEnumerable<object> is legal.

entries.plainDefinition: A consumer: T only appears in input positions, so a wider T can substitute for a narrower one.
entries.example: Action<object> assigned to Action<string> is legal.

entries.plainDefinition: No substitution allowed. List<string> is not compatible with List<object>.
entries.example: IList<T> is invariant because it both reads and writes T.

blocks.text: Variance lets you pass read-only sequences and callbacks without copying or wrapping. It also explains a classic interview trap: arrays are covariant (string[] to object[]) but can throw ArrayTypeMismatchException on write — generics fixed that for List<T>. TypeScript infers compatibility structurally and historically treated function parameters as bivariant. C# variance is declared with out/in on interfaces and checked by the compiler.

blocks.title: The mnemonic
blocks.body: out = output = covariant (producer widens). in = input = contravariant (consumer narrows). Mutable collections like IList<T> are invariant because T goes both directions.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Deciding if a conversion is legal

items.title: Check if the interface declares variance
items.body: Only interfaces and delegates with out T or in T participate. Classes and structs are always invariant.

items.title: Covariance: T only out
items.body: If every use of T is a return type or read-only output, out T allows substituting a derived type argument.

items.title: Contravariance: T only in
items.body: If every use of T is a parameter type, in T allows substituting a base type argument.

items.title: Value types do not convert
items.body: IEnumerable<int> cannot become IEnumerable<object> — int is a value type, not a reference type.

snippet.label: Covariance and contravariance
snippet.explanation: Read-only sequences can widen the element type (covariance). Mutating lists cannot (invariance). Callbacks that accept a wider input can be used where a narrower input is expected (contravariance).

snippet.label: Array covariance — the historical hole
snippet.explanation: Arrays are covariant for reference types but unsafe on write. Generic List<T> is invariant — the compiler rejects the bad assignment.

snippet.label: TypeScript comparison (conceptual)
snippet.explanation: TypeScript checks compatibility structurally. Enable strictFunctionTypes for contravariant callback parameters, closer to Action<in T>. C# variance is opt-in on interfaces and explicitly declared.

blocks.title: Variance rules across languages
rows: out T / in T on interfaces and delegates

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming List<string> is a List<object> — it is not. Declaring a variant interface that uses T in both input and output positions — the compiler rejects it. Citing array covariance as proof that List<T> is covariant. Importing TypeScript function bivariance into C# — they are different rules.

blocks.text: Variance is declared on **interfaces and delegates only** with out (covariant producer) and in (contravariant consumer). IList<T> is invariant because T appears in both input and output positions — assigning List<string> to List<object> would let you Add a Cat to a list of dogs. IEnumerable<out T> is covariant because you only read T. Action<in T> is contravariant because you only pass T in. Value types never participate: IEnumerable<int> cannot become IEnumerable<object>. Arrays are covariant for reference types but unsafe on write — ArrayTypeMismatchException. Generic sharing still applies under the hood, but variance is a compile-time assignability rule on reference types. How to prove it in production: code review grep for IList<object> = listOfStrings anti-pattern; enable TypeScript strictFunctionTypes when comparing to Action<in T>.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: T only in — consumer accepts wider input
T in and out — Add would break safety

snippet.label: Declaring variance on your own interface
snippet.explanation: The compiler validates that out T never appears in input positions and in T never in output positions. This is stricter than TypeScript structural rules.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying List<string> is assignable to List<object> — invariant, rejected at compile time. Claiming all generics are covariant because arrays are — arrays are the unsafe exception. Importing TypeScript bivariant function parameters into C# — use strictFunctionTypes for a fair comparison to Action<in T>. Strong answer: out producer, in consumer, IList invariant, value types excluded.

interviewTakeaways: out T = covariant producer (IEnumerable); in T = contravariant consumer (Action); classes and List<T> are invariant.
Value types do not participate in variant conversions — IEnumerable<int> is not IEnumerable<object>.
Arrays are covariant for reference elements but throw on bad writes; List<T> fixed that with invariance.

60s: out is covariant producer — IEnumerable<string> to IEnumerable<object>. in is contravariant consumer — Action<object> to Action<string>. IList and List are invariant. Value types excluded. Arrays are the historical unsafe exception.
Follow-up: why cannot you declare out T on an interface that accepts T in a method parameter?
commonPitfalls: Assuming List<string> is a List<object> — that assignment fails at compile time and rejects the answer.
Strong answer: List<T> is invariant; only interfaces/delegates with out/in participate in variance.
Declaring a variant interface that uses T in both input and output positions — compiler rejects it.
Citing array covariance as proof that List<T> is covariant — arrays are unsafe; generic lists are invariant.

jsTsCorrelations.note: strictFunctionTypes makes callback parameters contravariant, aligning with Action<in T>. ReadonlyArray is covariant like IEnumerable<out T>.
JavaScript has no out/in keywords. Assigning arrays or functions is structural and unchecked at run time — closer to the unsafe array covariance trap than to IList invariance.
